items.item: Item 1 (Part A): 3/4 __ 5/8, circle symbol, no work
items.elicits: Selecting the correct comparison symbol from three options with no work shown or required.

items.item: Item 2 (Part A): 2/3 __ 7/12, circle symbol, no work
items.elicits: Selecting the correct comparison symbol from three options with no work shown or required.

items.item: Item 3 (Part A): 5/6 __ 8/9, circle symbol, no work
items.elicits: Selecting the correct comparison symbol from three options with no work shown or required.

claims.narrower_inference: Students can select the correct comparison symbol for pairs of unlike fractions, with no evidence of the strategy used to get there.
claims.supports: Under these conditions, a teacher may conclude that a student can correctly judge the relative size of two unlike fractions and mark the right symbol.
does_not_support: Whether the student chose and executed a valid strategy (equivalent fractions, a benchmark such as one half, or a visual model), since Part A explicitly instructs 'Do not show work.'
Whether the student's reasoning actually supports the symbol, as the claim requires — no reasoning is collected anywhere for comparison items.
Guess-rate caveat: with three options (<, >, =) and no work required, a correct circle on any single item could reflect a 1-in-3 guess rather than genuine comparison skill.
Could be mistaken for full evidence of G5C1 (strategy execution and reasoning), when the item design captures only the endpoint judgment, not the process the claim names.

delegation.reason: Because no work is required, a correct symbol could come from genuine comparison reasoning or from a lucky guess, and the item cannot tell the two apart, though guessing all three correctly by chance is unlikely.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether students can choose and execute a valid comparison strategy or explain why it supports the symbol, since Part A withholds work and no other item requires a justified fraction comparison.

minimum_additional_observation.item_text: Compare 4/9 and 5/8 without finding a common denominator. Circle >, <, or =. Then write ONE sentence explaining how you know, using a benchmark (like one half) or equivalent fractions.
minimum_additional_observation.variant_rule: Keep one fraction below one half and the other above one half (or another shared property that makes a benchmark or equivalent-fraction shortcut genuinely available); change the specific fractions each period; avoid pairs that only yield to cross-multiplication with no shortcut, since the point is to surface a nameable strategy.
minimum_additional_observation.conditions: Proctored in class, individual, paper/pencil only, AI prohibited and enforced -- same conditions as the rest of the assessment; fractions not seen previously.
minimum_additional_observation.sufficiency_line: A response counts as evidence if the symbol is correct AND the one-line reason names the actual controlling feature used (e.g., 'both are close to one half' or 'same numerator so fewer, bigger pieces'), not just a restated answer.

items.elicits: Constructing a common denominator for two unlike fractions and combining the like-sized parts (result already in lowest terms, so no reduction is required).
Constructing a common denominator and combining like-sized parts by subtraction (result already in lowest terms).
Constructing common denominators for two mixed numbers, combining whole and fractional parts, and regrouping an improper fractional part into a whole (mixed-number regrouping).
Applying the common-denominator addition procedure inside a word-problem context and converting an improper result to a mixed number.
Applying the common-denominator subtraction procedure inside a word-problem context (result already in lowest terms, no regrouping or reduction required).

items.item: Item 9 (secondary bearing): correct sum for 1/2 + 1/4 after error repair
items.elicits: Re-executing the common-denominator addition procedure to produce a corrected sum (reinforces the combine step only; result already in lowest terms).

claims.narrower_inference: Students can construct a common denominator for unlike fractions (including mixed numbers), combine the resulting like-sized parts by addition or subtraction, and regroup an improper fractional part into a mixed number -- but not shown: reducing a sum or difference to lowest terms when the raw result is not already in simplest form, since every computed answer across the assessment already lands in lowest terms.
claims.supports: A teacher may conclude that a student can construct common denominators for unlike fractions and mixed numbers, combine like-sized parts by addition or subtraction, and regroup an improper fraction into a mixed number, under supervised, individual, resource-limited conditions with new numbers.
does_not_support: Whether the student can reduce a sum or difference to lowest terms when the raw result is not already in simplest form -- across items 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 every computed answer is already fully reduced, so the 'simplifies' component of the claim is never actually triggered despite the instruction 'answers in simplest form.'
Whether the student can compare (rather than combine) like-sized parts, the other half of the 'combines or compares' language -- that is exercised only in Part A, without work shown (see G5C1).
Nothing here distinguishes a student who checks for and reduces common factors from one who has never learned to, since no answer requires that check.
Could be mistaken for full evidence that students can 'simplify fractions,' a sub-skill this instrument names in the claim but never actually probes.

delegation.reason: Every item requires every step shown on paper under direct supervision with AI prohibited, so a correct multi-step written solution is very difficult to produce without actually performing the common-denominator and combination work.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether students can reduce a computed sum or difference to lowest terms, since none of the six items bearing on this claim produce a result that is not already in simplest form.

minimum_additional_observation.item_text: Three students already added or subtracted fractions and got these answers: 4/8, 5/9, 6/10. Circle the ones that are NOT written in simplest form, then rewrite each circled one in simplest form.
minimum_additional_observation.variant_rule: Include at least one answer already in simplest form as a distractor and at least two reducible fractions with different common factors (e.g., one reducible by 2, one by 3); change the specific fractions each period; keep denominators within the range already practised (through 12).
minimum_additional_observation.conditions: Proctored in class, individual, paper/pencil only, AI prohibited and enforced -- same conditions as the rest of the assessment; fractions not seen previously.
minimum_additional_observation.sufficiency_line: A response counts as evidence if the student correctly identifies every non-simplest fraction AND rewrites each in true lowest terms, not just a smaller-looking but still reducible form.

items.item: Item 9 (Part D): student added 1/2 + 1/4 and got 2/6; explain the error and show the correct answer
items.elicits: Identifying and naming the specific misconception in an unfamiliar incorrect solution (adding denominators as well as numerators) and executing the correct common-denominator procedure to repair it.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude that a student can recognize the 'add the denominators' error in an unfamiliar incorrect solution and produce the correct sum via proper common-denominator addition, under supervised, individual, resource-limited conditions with a new instance of this error.
does_not_support: Whether the student's written explanation names the conceptual reason (that adding denominators changes the size of the piece being counted) rather than only a procedural fix such as 'should have found a common denominator' -- the item invites but does not force the size-based reasoning the claim's wording specifies.
Whether the student would catch this same error type presented in a different guise (e.g., inside a word problem, or in a subtraction rather than an addition).

Whether this exact error is absent from the student's own unprompted computation elsewhere on the test -- this item tests recognition in someone else's work, not the presence or absence of the error in the student's own spontaneous work.
Could be mistaken for a guarantee that the student would never make this error themselves under different conditions, when it only shows they can diagnose it when it is presented to them.

delegation.reason: The item requires a written explanation plus a full corrected computation on paper under direct supervision with AI prohibited, which is difficult to produce convincingly without actually locating and repairing the error.

claims.why_no_intervention: This claim is already carried directly: item 9 is a Diagnose item matching the claim almost verbatim (locate the adding-denominators error, give the correct sum), run under supervised, individual, novel conditions with AI excluded. Adding another item would duplicate existing verification without buying additional evidence.

conditions_echo: Proctored in class, individual, AI prohibited and enforced, paper and pencil only, summative, 25 minutes, end of Unit 4; the item types have been practised but these specific numbers and problems are new to students.
reviewer_notes: Parts B, C and D produce strong independent, novel, claim-targeted evidence for G5C2 and G5C3, with 'show every step' and the Diagnose item doing real work. The two substantive design gaps both come from the same pattern -- a sub-skill is named in a claim and implied by an instruction, but no item actually forces it to appear: Part A's 'Do not show work' forecloses the strategy-and-reasoning half of G5C1 even though the symbol judgment is well covered, and every computed answer across Parts B, C and D already happens to be in lowest terms, so 'simplifies' in G5C2 is instructed for but never tested. Both are named, bounded, and each gets exactly one short supervised add-on; nothing else in the instrument needs to change.
